title: A Young Man at Twilight
summary: The father urges his son to treasure his commandments and to call wisdom his sister, so that he will be kept from the adulteress. Then he tells what he saw from his window: a young man without sense wandering near a woman's house at dusk, met by her in the street, persuaded by her invitation while her husband is away, and following her like an ox to the slaughter. The chapter ends by warning that her house is the road to Sheol.
story: This is the third and fullest warning about the forbidden woman in chapters 5 to 7. Chapter 5 described her costs, chapter 6 compared adultery to embracing fire, and chapter 7 now dramatizes a single evening from start to finish. The story prepares directly for chapters 8 and 9, where two women call out to the simple: Wisdom, whose house leads to life, and Folly, whose guests are in the depths of Sheol. The adulteress of chapter 7, who seizes a young man in the street, is the living picture of what Folly will say in 9:13-18.
historical:
No historical event stands behind the story; it is a teaching narrative, a scene the father describes as though he watched it happen. Its details, though, reflect real life in an Israelite town. Peace offerings (verse 14) were sacrifices described in Leviticus 3 and 7, in which part of the animal was burned on the altar, part given to the priest, and the rest eaten by the worshiper and their household. Leviticus 7:15-18 required the meat of a vow or freewill offering to be eaten within a day or two. The woman's claim that she has paid her vows means she has fresh meat at home and a feast ready, a rare luxury for most people.

The linen from Egypt, myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon (verses 16 and 17) were expensive imported goods that reached Israel by trade routes from Egypt, Arabia, and farther east. They signal wealth and a carefully prepared seduction. Her husband's absence with a bag of money, not due back until the full moon (verses 19 and 20), suggests a merchant on a trading trip and assures the young man that no one will catch them.
cultural:
Houses in ancient Israelite towns often had small windows covered by lattices of wood, which let in air and light while allowing people inside to look out without being seen. The father's vantage point at such a window makes him an unseen witness. The time of day matters too: twilight and the first dark of night were when streets emptied, and there was no street lighting, so a young man strolling near a woman's corner at that hour was putting himself where he had no business being.

The woman's dress and behavior mark her out. The attire of a harlot, her loud and defiant manner, and her habit of lurking in streets and squares rather than staying home all broke the expectations of a married woman in that culture. Calling wisdom your sister (verse 4) used the language of family intimacy and possibly of affection (sister is also used of a bride in the Song of Songs). The father wants his son to be so close to wisdom that the stranger's advances have no room.
literary: The chapter is framed by instruction (verses 1 to 5 and 24 to 27) around a vivid narrative (verses 6 to 23). The story is told like a short drama: the setting (a window, a street, the fall of night), the characters (the watching father, the naive youth, the prepared woman), a long speech by the woman in verses 14 to 20 full of religious, sensual, and practical reassurances, and a swift ending told in three animal similes, an ox to the slaughter, a deer into a trap, a bird into a snare. The pace slows as the woman speaks and then accelerates as the young man follows. The house motif ties it together: the father's house, the woman's house, and finally her house as the road to Sheol and the chambers of death.

outline.t: Keep my words and call wisdom your sister
From my window: a young man at dusk
The woman meets him and makes her offer
He follows like an ox to the slaughter
Her house is the road to Sheol

doctrines.note: The story shows temptation step by step: carelessness about where you go, a moment of opportunity, persuasive words, and a decision made on impulse. The young man is described as lacking judgment long before he meets the woman.

The antidote to seduction is intimacy with wisdom, keeping God's commands as closely as the pupil of the eye and treating wisdom like a sister. Protection comes from what a person loves, not only from what they avoid.
The chapter closes by saying that the woman has brought many down to death and her house leads to Sheol. The consequences of sin are real and can be final, whatever the invitation promises.

words.note: Ishon, pupil of the eye, translated apple of your eye in verse 2. The word is usually explained as a diminutive meaning little man, perhaps from the tiny reflection a person sees of himself in another's eye. It names the most sensitive and instinctively protected part of the body. God's commands are to be guarded with that same reflex.

Bayit, house or home. It appears six times in the chapter and structures the story: the father looks out from his house, the young man drifts toward hers, she assures him that her husband is not at home and won't come home for days, and the chapter ends by saying her house is the road to Sheol. Where a person goes in shows where they are headed.

Nephesh, soul or life. It means the whole living person, not a separate spiritual part. In verse 23 the young man doesn't realize that the evening will cost him his very life. The word gives the story its final, sobering weight.

christ: The New Testament describes the dynamics of this chapter in its own words. James 1:14-15 says each person is tempted when lured and enticed by his own desire, and desire, once conceived, gives birth to sin, and sin, when full grown, brings death, a close summary of the young man's evening. Paul promises that God provides a way of escape in temptation (1 Corinthians 10:13), and he tells Timothy to flee youthful passions (2 Timothy 2:22). Hebrews 4:15 says Jesus was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin, so he is able to sympathize and to help. Where the young man of Proverbs 7 wandered without sense, Jesus faced temptation in the wilderness and answered it with the word of God (Matthew 4:1-11), the very thing the father urges his son to keep.

hard.q: Why does the woman mention sacrifices and vows just before inviting the young man to her bed?
hard.a: Her words in verse 14 are one of the chapter's most unsettling details. At the simplest level they explain the feast: peace offerings left the worshiper with meat that had to be eaten quickly, so she has a banquet ready. But the mention also shows how easily religious practice can sit alongside, and even dress up, a plan to sin. She has kept her vows at the sanctuary and in the same breath proposes adultery. Some scholars have suggested the scene reflects foreign cults in which sacred rites and sexual activity were linked, and some see the woman as a symbol of idolatry itself, since the prophets often describe unfaithfulness to God as adultery. Others think the passage is simply exposing religious hypocrisy of an ordinary kind. The text doesn't settle which, but its warning is clear: outward religious observance is no guarantee of a faithful heart.

questions: The young man was near the woman's corner at dusk before anything happened. What small choices of place, time, or company make temptation easier for you?
What does it mean in practice to call wisdom your sister, to be that close to it?
The woman uses religious language to reassure the young man. How can religious practice become a cover for sin rather than a check on it?
